On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.
papers.comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Supplementary material (13 pages) included as an ancillary file

papers.title: Electrically Pumped Quadratic-Soliton Mode-Locked Laser in Lithium Niobate Nanophotonics
papers.summary: Femtosecond mode-locked lasers are the workhorse of modern photonics, enabling optical atomic clocks, frequency combs, precision spectroscopy, and ultrafast signal processing. Bringing them onto nanophotonic chips promises miniaturized ultrafast systems, yet combining femtosecond pulse generation with electrical pumping remains a major challenge, rooted in a trade-off between the speed and energy efficiency of mode-locking mechanisms. Kerr-based mechanisms offer nearly instantaneous response but typically require high intracavity peak powers that are difficult to achieve with nanophotonic-compatible semiconductor gain. Conversely, semiconductor saturable absorbers enable strong nonlinear responses at low energies but are limited by their slow carrier dynamics. Here we break this trade-off by introducing quadratic-soliton mode-locking based on a quadratic nonlinear interferometer (QNLI): an effective saturable absorber built from cascaded second-order nonlinearity in periodically poled lithium niobate nanophotonics, with a measured sub-20 fs response time. Through hybrid integration with an electrically pumped semiconductor gain element, we demonstrate a self-starting quadratic-soliton mode-locked laser with femtojoule pulse energies, operating in single- and multiple-soliton states. Quadratic solitons arise through the QNLI's dissipative and dispersive nonlinear response, which we confirm with a modified complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in agreement with measurements. By combining soliton formation with intracavity electro-optic modulation, we generate 750 fs pulses with flat-top spectra. Our engineerable, ultra-energy-efficient, electrically powered laser provides the critical source for fully integrated ultrafast photonic circuits in lithium niobate nanophotonics that natively offers electro-optic control, quadratic wavelength conversion, pulse compression, and spectral broadening.

papers.title: The Dynamics of RMSProp Beyond the Stability Threshold
papers.summary: We study what happens to RMSProp when the learning rate is too large for convergence to the minimizer. For positive-definite quadratic loss functions, we show that the minimizer is Lyapunov un- stable above an explicit critical learning rate. Nevertheless, every trajectory eventually enters a compact trapping region. We obtain explicit bounds proportional to h in the spatial variables and to h2 in the memory variables, where h is the learning rate. We also prove that nontrivial period-two orbits exist precisely above the critical learning rate, and under additional spectral assumptions, an attracting branch of these orbits emerges from the minimizer. For sufficiently large learning rates, we construct branches near admissible corners of a cube. We then explore the dynamics inside the trapping region using the parameterization method and numerical continuation, exploring invariant circles and tori, coexistence of attracting sets, circle-doubling sequences, and chaotic motions. We examine how the dynamics depend on the loss Hessian, memory decay, and dimension. Finally, we test a learning-rate reduction schedule and continue selected invariant circles into an autonomous variant of the Adam optimizer.

papers.title: A linear, second-order, unconditionally energy-stable scalar-auxiliary-variable scheme for the CHQ viscoelastic phase-separation model
papers.summary: The CHQ model describes viscoelastic phase separation in a polymer--solvent mixture: a Cahn--Hilliard equation for the polymer volume fraction $φ$ is two-way coupled, through a phase-dependent cross-diffusion flux, to a damped relaxation equation for a scalar bulk elastic stress $q$. We propose a scalar-auxiliary-variable (SAV) time discretisation of this system, combining the SAV reformulation of the double-well potential with a second-order backward differentiation formula (BDF2) and a second-order extrapolation of all phase-dependent mobilities: a linear, computationally cheaper complement to the reference scheme's fully nonlinear Newton solve. The resulting method is (i) linear at every time step, with a coupling structure we prove has exactly one solution at every step, for every choice of time-step size; (ii) mass conserving, exactly, as an algebraic identity of the discrete equations themselves (the only drift ever seen numerically traces to the finite tolerance of the iterative linear solver, not a failure of the conservation property); and (iii) unconditionally stable for a modified discrete energy, via an exact one-step energy--dissipation identity. We show the energy identity extends to this filtered variant as well, with two explicit extra non-negative terms. Hence, the scheme actually producing the physics results is itself provably stable for the same energy. A Fourier--Galerkin implementation verifies that the energy identity holds at every time step to within floating-point round-off. It also confirms second-order temporal accuracy, including in the steep-interface regime, and agreement with an independently implemented nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver. Compared with that independent nonlinear Newton--BDF2 solver, at equal grid resolution, the SAV method uses $2.5$--$3.0\times$ fewer linear-solver iterations and $1.7$--$2.0\times$ less wall-clock time.

papers.title: Circuits of LLM Classifiers
papers.summary: Language models make it easy to build classifiers by simply prompting a model with the sample to classify. However, their predictions are neither deterministic nor uniformly reliable across samples. How can we combine predictions from different models to improve reliability? We view LLM classifiers as noisy measurement instruments of an underlying target label. Our goal is to maximize average classification accuracy at a given average query cost. To this end, we introduce circuits that organize LLM classifiers into an adaptive sequence of queries and decisions. We then characterize the optimal circuit, obtain the fundamental limits of achievable accuracy, and provide practical insights on realizing the optimal circuit. Across seven classification tasks spanning safety, health, political science, human preference, agent evaluation, decision-making and reasoning, our method improves the cost-accuracy frontier over routing and cascading baselines.

papers.title: From Classifier Heads to Encoder Prototypes: Personalized Federated Learning with Head-Derived Clustering
papers.summary: Personalized federated learning must decide which clients should share representations. We introduce HDC-FL (Head-Derived Clustering for Personalized Federated Learning), which reads that decision off a signal shared-encoder training already produces: the client-specific classifi- er heads. At periodic refresh rounds the server projects the cached heads into a normalized low-rank descriptor space, groups the descriptors, builds one encoder prototype per group from the cached client encoders, and returns to each client a soft mixture of those prototypes paired with its own unchanged head. Client-specific heads are never averaged or distributed to oth- er clients; the shared-encoder trajectory is left intact; and no second optimization trajectory, additional local objective, or post-training fine-tuning stage is required. Across 11 CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 configurations covering label-subset, Dirichlet and rotation heterogeneity with ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2 encoders, HDC-FL is competitive with the strongest personalized and clustered baselines in macro-averaged mean accuracy and attains the numerically highest macro-averaged worst-client and bottom-20% accuracy among the evaluated methods. The tail results distinguish methods that look similar when only their means are compared. A controlled donor-swap diagnostic further finds positive donor-ranking associations between head similarity and encoder compatibility in all three settings tested, most clearly under covariate shift.

papers.title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
papers.summary: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/χ_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $χ_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.

papers.title: When Windowed Anderson Acceleration Converges Faster
papers.summary: Windowed Anderson acceleration AA($m$) combines at most $m+1$ recent iterates by least squares. For a real affine contraction $x\mapsto Wx+b$ with $q=\|W\| \in(0,1)$, we determine exactly when AA($m$) converges from every starting point with an asymptotic factor below $q$. We give a polynomial criterion for this improvement and an equivalent spectral condition: there is no probability distribution on the phases of the eigenvalues of modulus $q$ whose first $m$ cosine moments are $q,q^2,\ldots,q^m$. If such a distribution exists, we construct a starting point from which AA($m$) reproduces fixed-point iteration at every step. Otherwise, over a fixed number of consecutive steps, every run contracts the residual norm by a common factor strictly smaller than the corresponding power of $q$. The polynomial criterion also gives explicit convergence-rate bounds with constants independent of the dimension. When $q$ equals the spectral radius, this characterizes improvement over the asymptotic convergence factor of fixed-point iteration. For general affine contractions, the asymptotic factor never exceeds the numerical radius of $W$, and a related moment condition gives a uniform upper bound strictly below that radius.

papers.title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
papers.summary: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

papers.title: Inaccessibility of the Cosmological Singularity to Quantum Probes
papers.summary: We propose an operational resolution of the FLRW big bang singularity using quantum probes satisfying a curvature coupled Klein-Gordon equation. Applying the Madelung-Bohm decomposition of a Klein-Gordon field on a classical near-singularity FLRW background, we show that the induced conformal geometry renders curvature invariants finite and makes past directed causal geodesics complete. The classical big bang surface is therefore inaccessible to this class of quantum probes in finite effective proper time, while the underlying FLRW spacetime remains singular.

papers.title: A random sampling method to test the weak Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis
papers.summary: We introduce a random sampling method for testing the weak Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (wETH) that is particularly useful for large, sparse Hamiltonians. We test the method on a well-studied Rydberg atom system that exhibits both two- and three-body dipole-dipole interactions. Our results show that our method allows for the study of system sizes significantly beyond the limits of exact diagonalization. We find that the fluctuations in eigenstate expectation values decay as the Hilbert space dimension $D^{-1/2}$, consistent with wETH and in agreement with previous numerical results.

papers.title: Alternative moduli of twisted curves
papers.summary: We define new Artin stack compactifications of the moduli of smooth curves, which parameterize "relatively polarized curves" consisting of stacky semistable curves equipped with line bundles that are trivialized away from the rational bridges. Using techniques from birational geometry, we prove that stacks of relatively polarized curves admit the classical coarse space $\overline{M}_g$ of stable curves as a good moduli space. One of our main motivations is a companion paper where we construct a proper moduli space of $\mathrm{SL}_N$-bundles on relatively polarized curves. This suggests the hypothesis that relatively polarized curves are suitable sources for defining Gromov-Witten theory for Artin stack targets.

papers.title: Loopholing All the Way: Language Modeling with pure Self-Conditioning
papers.summary: Recent Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) use Self-Conditioning (SC), or Loopholing, to improve their performance. While SC is traditionally seen as an auxiliary heuristic, its empirical success raises the question: can a continuous generative model be based purely on Self-Conditioning? We answer affirmatively with LAW (``Loopholing All the Way''), which propagates the Expected Embedding under the denoiser's prediction across steps, decoding the tokens once, at the end. On Sudoku, LAW outperforms previous Discrete and Continuous Diffusion Models, including Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. On Maze, LAW is the most accurate from 2 to 64 NFE. After training on TinyGSM and sampling at temperature 1 with 1024 NFE, LAW solves 42.2% of GSM8K problems against 34.5% for uniform Loopholing Discrete Diffusion. Additionally, fine-tuning a pre-trained Uniform Diffusion Model (Duo) with LAW increases its accuracy from 17.2% to 48.1%. Finally, on OpenWebText, LAW pushes the Pareto frontier and approaches Autoregressive Models (ARMs) with 64 NFE. Find our code at https://github.com/ilievanadezhda/law.

papers.title: GoiBERT: Compact Vietnamese Language Models via Two-Stage Knowledge Distillation
papers.summary: Vietnamese pre-trained encoders have improved rapidly, but the strongest ones are large, multilingual-vocabulary models or depend on external word segmentation, which makes them costly to deploy. We present GoiBERT, a family of two compact Vietnamese encoders with 26M and 49M parameters that operate directly on raw text. GoiBERT learns from two complementary teachers. A same-tokenizer Vietnamese encoder first teaches general-purpose representations. A much larger teacher then provides task-level guidance through soft labels that are generated without ever labeling its own training data. Across eight benchmarks covering text classification, aspect-based sentiment analysis, natural language inference, and named entity recognition, GoiBERT-large achieves the highest average score among non-teacher models. It does so with fewer than half the parameters of the strongest compact baseline and twice its throughput. GoiBERT-base retains 99% of that baseline's performance at a quarter of its size. Our analysis shows that compression is nearly lossless for sentiment and classification tasks but remains costly for inference and entity recognition, which points to clear directions for future work. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/Nhantran65/GoiBERT.git

papers.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising sequences of ordinary vocabulary tokens, any of which may be corrupted and subsequently revised. During training, UDLMs must denoise from a context that may itself be unreliable, whereas masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) always condition on a clean context. This challenging training objective makes UDLMs more FLOP-intensive to train than MDLMs, but it yields stronger downstream reasoning performance. Recently, selective looping, which recursively applies a few early Transformer layers within each denoising step, has been shown to improve training efficiency in MDLMs under an iso-FLOP budget. We investigate looping in UDLMs while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged. We find that looping significantly improves training efficiency: looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of a non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8x fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3x fewer on FineWeb-Edu. We also find that, at a matched NFE budget, looped UDLMs reach up to 9.8% lower generation perplexity than the non-looped UDLM, with most gains achieved at moderate loop counts. Finally, we study different loop-count distributions and find that sampling smaller loop counts more frequently during training improves inference efficiency: on downstream tasks, this strategy uses 12% fewer loops than uniform loop-count sampling without degrading accuracy.

papers.title: Reflection functors for non-simply-laced quiver varieties
papers.summary: We prove the braid relations between reflection functors on non-simply-laced analogues of Nakajima quiver varieties, which are defined as critical loci of certain quivers with potential. We extend this framework to categories of matrix factorizations and critical $K$-theory.

papers.title: Post-adiabatic effective-one-body waveforms for coalescing compact binaries
papers.summary: I apply and extend the formalism of osculating orbits of Damour et al. (2004) and Lynch et al. (2026) to eccentric effective one body (EOB) models, in order to obtain an efficient yet accurate description of the inspiral-to-plunge dynamics of tidal, spinning compact binaries, including precessing ones by twisting the otherwise planar motion. The method is recast in terms of equinoctial orbital elements, to circumvent singularities associated with the zero-eccentricity limit. While the formalism is general and can be applied to any EOB model, I focus here on the TEOBResumS-Dalí family and demonstrate how this technique speeds up waveform generation without significantly compromising the accuracy of the model. Over $10^4$ binary neutron stars (BNSs) and as many binary black holes (BBHs) with initial eccentricities up to $0.6$ at $20$ Hz, the median speedup against an optimized version of the model is $\sim 2.6$ for BNSs and $\sim 1.5$ for BBHs, with mismatches against the full numerical solution always below $5 \times 10^{-7}$. The largest speedups, up to $\sim 7$ for individual systems, are obtained for light BBHs ($M \lesssim 8 M_\odot$) with low eccentricities $(e_0 \lesssim 0.1)$. In absolute terms, the median time needed to generate a BNS waveform is $\sim 0.5$ s, with $99.7\%$ of the systems below one second, and for long signals the model is up to $\sim 26$ times faster than a previous version. Applied to the calculation of initial conditions in the $e \rightarrow 0$ limit, the inclusion of radiation-reaction effects allows the model's input eccentricity to agree with the gauge-invariant waveform eccentricity down to initial values of $\sim 7 \times 10^{-8}$. Beyond time-domain applications, the same construction also gives frequency-domain EOB waveforms for eccentric compact binaries via a multi-harmonic stationary phase approximation.

papers.title: On the proof of the Kozma-Nitzan conjecture
papers.summary: In this short note, we give an exposition of the recent proof of the Kozma-Nitzan conjecture provided by OpenAI.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic description of correlation matrix eigenvalues in a finite temperature expanding free fermionic gas
papers.summary: A recent work considered the Page curve for entanglement entropy of a freely expanding one-dimensional Fermi gas starting from a finite box (the system) in a zero-temperature initial state that then expands in to a semi-infinite vacuum (the environment). For the case with a single defect at the system-environment junction, it was shown that the Yang-Yang entropy of the system computed from semiclassical hydrodynamics agrees with the microscopically computed entanglement entropy, yielding the Page curve. On the other hand, the environment Yang-Yang entropy showed a monotonic increase. Here, we propose a hydrodynamic description to obtain the eigenvalues of the microscopic correlation matrix for a nonzero temperature freely-expanding Fermi gas. For the system, the phase space density directly gives the correlation matrix eigenvalues and thus, via the Yang-Yang formula, yields the von-Neumann entropy. For the reservoir, a modification of the phase space density is required in the Yang-Yang formula, to incorporate coherences, in order to reproduce accurately the entropy. The hydrodynamic description of correlation matrix eigenvalues also leads to a Levitov-Lesovik type formula for the full-counting-statistics for a finite system in the transient regime. We provide a heuristic derivation of the correlation matrix eigenvalues based on a semiclassical wave-packet picture.

papers.title: Test-Time Motion Steering for Perceptive Humanoid Fall Recovery
papers.summary: Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/

papers.title: Facets of the X-ray polytope of doubly stochastic matrices
papers.summary: We study the polytope of anti-diagonal X-rays of k x k doubly stochastic matrices, the image of the Birkhoff polytope under the map that sums the entries along each anti-diagonal. Its facets other than the coordinate facets are the minimal joint tail bounds for lattice laws of a sum of two dependent uniform random variables. We give an exact facet criterion in terms of the allowed edges of a tight graph. For rays of the underlying tropical fan, total support of the tight graph suffices for a facet but is not necessary, as an example with k=19 shows. Up to affine functions and positive scaling, the potentials that define a facet form a polytope whose vertices are its rays. Facets propagate by padding and by grid refinement under explicit hypotheses. We give infinite families of facets from no step potential, facets of quadratic height, superpolynomially many facets, and a classification of three-step potentials. Total support of a step potential is characterized by a Hall-type condition on block starts; with computer assistance, total support decides facets of step potentials for k<=26. The facet counts up to k=12 are found directly for k<=3 and, for k>=4, come from an enumeration by a provably complete algorithm; an independent exact recomputation reproduces its ray lists for 5<=k<=12.
papers.comment: 36 pages, 4 tables; supplementary material (25 pages) as an ancillary file. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23440726 (https://github.com/methodtrace/2026-doubly-stochastic-xray-facets). Companion paper: arXiv:2610.24197

papers.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

papers.title: NLOS-Aware TDOA-Based UAV Localization: Cramér-Rao Bounds, Measurement Modeling, and Experimental Validation
papers.summary: Passive time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) localization is well suited for tracking non-cooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that do not report their positions. However, its accuracy degrades under the mixed line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) propagation that is typical of low-altitude flight. In this paper, we develop NLOS-aware Cramér--Rao lower bounds (CRLBs) and an empirically calibrated measurement model for TDOA-based UAV localization, and we evaluate both with measurements from five UAV flights on the Aerial Experimentation and Research Platform for Advanced Wireless (AERPAW). The analysis yields an identifiability condition that relates the number of sensors to the number of NLOS links, together with a bias-induced error floor that a wider bandwidth cannot remove. The model parameters are estimated by matching simulated and measured error distributions. Experimental results show that the error depends most strongly on the number of sensors in LOS, while a higher altitude and a wider bandwidth lower the median error. Relocating a sensor that is always in NLOS into the open flight area can lower the median horizontal bound by two orders of magnitude if the relocated sensor is in LOS. The fitted model reproduces the median errors of the 2.5 MHz and 5 MHz flights but underestimates the heaviest error tails. Finally, rejecting outlier fixes lowers the error far more than Kalman or particle filtering, because the remaining error is dominated by bias.
papers.comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems (TAES) on October 21st, 2026

papers.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
papers.summary: We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $Θ(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $Ω(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

papers.title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks
papers.summary: Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. Our framework enables models to control a robot directly through visual observations, robot proprioception, and structured tool calls, primarily by specifying target end-effector poses and gripper commands, without task-specific fine-tuning or pretrained manipulation skills. We evaluate six frontier AI models, including GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini-4 Argon, across three reasoning effort levels, resulting in 18 configurations and 1,800 evaluation episodes. Our results show that GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest success rate of 44%, followed by Gemini-4 Argon at 43%. Increasing reasoning effort generally improves manipulation performance, but the benefits vary across models and come at additional inference cost. We also observe substantial differences across tasks, with models performing relatively well on object placement tasks but struggling with precise spatial arrangements and complex multi-step interactions. These findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of frontier AI models for robot manipulation, highlighting the challenges of translating reasoning capabilities into reliable physical actions. We release our evaluation framework and experimental results to support reproducible benchmarking and future research on reasoning-based robot manipulation.
papers.comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. May Espinola and Qifan Zhang contributed equally. Project page: https://irvlutd.github.io/LLM-LIBERO/ Code: https://github.com/IRVLUTD/LLM_LIBERO

papers.title: On OpenAI's proof of the Nagata conjecture
papers.summary: These notes are an expanded account of my talk at UMass Amherst on OpenAI's remarkably simple proof of the Nagata conjecture. I hope they will be useful, especially to non-experts. The standard reduction to the normal cone and the collision of fat points into one monomial scheme reduce the problem to interpolation of monomial schemes on the normal ruled surface of a smooth plane cubic. The novelty is that the study of the asymptotics of theta functions as the cubic develops a node, together with interpolation duality, reduces the problem further to interpolation on a triangle of lattice points, which is straightforward. The same calculation determines the nef and pseudoeffective cones of a weighted blow-up of ${\Bbb P}^2$ at one point for very general local parameters when the ratio of weights is greater than nine.

papers.title: Exceptional points and hysteresis in Kerr-Newman quasi-normal modes
papers.summary: Exceptional points (EPs) and eigenstate hysteresis, previously found in Kerr only with an auxiliary scalar field, arise intrinsically in the quasinormal-mode spectrum of Kerr-Newman black holes. Using a hyperboloidal formulation of the coupled gravito-electromagnetic Teukolsky equations and a Chebyshev pseudospectral method, we compute the $\ell=m=2$ spectrum and locate four EPs at up to $99.974\%$ of extremality, one from a new repulsion. The gaps close as a square root branch point, and quasistatic loops around one or more EPs exchange the coalescing modes, confirming hysteresis.

papers.title: Projective symmetry groups beyond spin-$1/2$: Classifying integer-spin quantum spin liquids
papers.summary: Wen's projective symmetry group (PSG), introduced a quarter of a century ago, reduced the classification of symmetric quantum spin liquids to an algebraic problem and has guided the study of spin-$1/2$ models and materials ever since. Many current candidate materials and quantum simulators, however, have spin-$1$ or larger moments, and no comparable classification exists for them. We formulate the PSG for fermionic partons of arbitrary spin $S$. Integer and half-odd-integer spins already differ in their gauge structure. Half-odd-integer spins give the familiar $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, $\mathrm{U}(1)$, and $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant gauge groups, while integer spins give a different hierarchy that includes $\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$; the latter has no spin-$1/2$ counterpart. Three lattice-independent results follow for integer spin. Singlet pairing of the partons is odd under site exchange. A lattice symmetry can exchange the particle and hole representations of the local constraint, which forces symmetry-related sites into opposite constraint sectors. And a time-reversal-symmetric $\mathrm{U}(1)$ state with the same constraint on every site can be gapped only if the number of sites per unit cell is a multiple of $2S+1$. We apply the formalism to the spin-$1$ diamond lattice, realized in frustrated A-site spinels, and find ten fully symmetric Ansätze up to second neighbors. In the $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model at the mean-field level, the ground state depends on how the constraint is imposed. With the particle and hole representations, the lowest states are fully gapped $\mathrm{U}(1)$ states whose two sublattices sit in opposite constraint sectors, and one of them is gauge equivalent to a paired Ansatz. The classification provides a starting point for integer-spin quantum spin liquids on other lattices and in other materials.

papers.title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
papers.summary: Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill. To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).
papers.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Grounded User Simulation for Model Evaluation and Training: Diversity, Fidelity, and Validity'' (non-archival)

papers.title: Relative geometry of nuclear mean fields through differential forms
papers.summary: Proton and neutron densities can have similar multipole moments while differing locally. We use differential forms to measure and locate such differences between nuclear mean fields. A pair invariant measures the angle between two density gradients, weighted by their magnitudes, and the coarea formula resolves its contribution over level surfaces. A triple invariant factorizes exactly into a weighted pair term and a directional term that measures the variation of a third field along the level-surface intersections. We test these quantities in 98 magnetized Wigner-Seitz solutions, five static Hartree-Fock configurations, an illustrative $^{16}$O + $^{34}$Mg collision, and periodic nuclear pasta (a slab and a connected network). The pair invariant distinguishes cell solutions with comparable proton quadrupole moments and is 253 times larger in $^{34}$Mg than in $^{24}$Mg; refinement to 0.6 fm changes it by at most 1.3% in the four configurations recomputed. The directional factor separates the sampled triaxial configurations from the prolate ones. In the collision, it accounts for the 7.3-fold rise of the triple before the first recorded low-density connection, while the weighted pair term changes by at most 3%. In nuclear pasta, slab and network configurations have similar integrated proton-neutron misalignment but different distributions over density levels; their triple invariants differ by a factor of about 370 on the finer grid, mainly due to the variation of the Coulomb potential along joint density levels. These comparisons require no preferred origin or axis. A resolved nonzero triple excludes a common symmetry axis, but zero does not establish one. The pasta results require further convergence studies.
papers.comment: 16 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to Physical Review C. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23460790

papers.title: Which Differences Matter? Controlled Tests of Rule Transfer, Joint Reliability, and Information Use in Decision Models
papers.summary: Decision models map stated rules and observed states to discrete answers. Aggregate accuracy leaves unresolved which rule and information changes guide those answers. We connect controlled input changes to transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use through executable arithmetic rules. Semantic rule separation and crossed rule and state tests make transfer and joint success separately measurable. We compare equivalent wordings, calibrate joint correctness through marginal-preserving reassociation, and alter tables to define alternative answer targets. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement; fully conflicting quartets yield small pooled gains and different gain signs across source splits. Equivalent rewrites have opposing task-level effects, linking transfer gains to rule presentation. Joint-score departures depend on which rule and state associations the reference preserves. A decision service changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and usually follows the answer targets implied by altered table values or mappings.

papers.title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our \href{https://sp-hlm.github.io/}{\textcolor{blue}{project page}}.

papers.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
papers.summary: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://xuyicheng-zju.github.io/TARSphere/ Code: https://github.com/xuyicheng-zju/TARSphere

papers.title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
papers.summary: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants' final performance with 2x-4x fewer evaluation budget.

papers.title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents
papers.summary: Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10\% of trajectory positions capture 96.12\% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36\% with full trajectory to 36.79\%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10\% localized positions achieves 57.38\%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills.

papers.title: An entanglement band structure for general multiqubit states
papers.summary: Majorana drew a symmetric multiqubit state as points on the Bloch sphere, antipodal to the zeros of its overlap with spin coherent states. Projecting only one qubit of a general state leaves the others in a state that varies with direction. Its entanglement invariants are eigenvalues of a non-Hermitian matrix and form bands over the sphere. Exceptional points appear, without gain or loss, where the entanglement family of the rest changes. Circling one exchanges two bands, so the bands form one Riemann surface. At five qubits it fixes the entanglement class up to finitely many choices.

papers.title: Unlocking the Full Potential of Taylor Dispersion Analysis Through Advanced Detection
papers.summary: Today, pharmaceutical sciences rely on a wide range of innovative therapeutics of varying sizes: nanoparticles, proteins, antibodies, and nanocarriers for drug delivery. Measuring their size is one of the crucial parameters in their characterization, to ensure drug safety, stability, and effectiveness. Over the past two decades, Taylor Dispersion Analysis has emerged as an important sizing method. Its scope of application is perfectly suited to the sizes of these therapeutics. By design, it can be coupled with a wide range of detectors, and extensive research has been conducted in this field. In this review, we will present an overview of the studies conducted, and discuss how the application drives the choice of one detector or another (size measurement, aggregation studies, interaction studies, and other analyses, performed in both simple biological buffers and in more complex media, particularly serum) and makes Taylor Dispersion Analysis a highly versatile tool.

papers.title: Long-time dynamics of viscous Gröbli triangles
papers.summary: In 1877 Gröbli discovered that three point vortices in the plane can move self-similarly, forming a triangle that rotates while either expanding indefinitely or collapsing in finite time. We study the viscous counterpart of these configurations, namely the two-dimensional Navier--Stokes evolution starting from three point vortices arranged in a Gröbli triangle. In the expanding case, viscosity spreads the vortex cores at the same rate as the triangle grows, so the vortices remain well separated relative to their size. Building on this observation, we show that at high Reynolds number the solution stays close to three Lamb--Oseen vortices centered near the vertices of the inviscid triangle for times that grow exponentially with a power of the Reynolds number. In the collapsing case, the same description holds up to times close to the inviscid collision. As an application of the long-time result in the expanding case, we obtain a vanishing viscosity realization of the vortex burst, a nonuniqueness mechanism for point vortices in which a single vortex splits into an expanding Gröbli triangle.
papers.comment: 68 pages, 4 figures, SageMath script in the supplementary material

papers.title: Attn-Forcing: Learning Full-Context Attention Proxies for Streaming Video Generation
papers.summary: Increasing the attention context length significantly improves streaming video generation quality, while incurring prohibitive memory and computational costs as the context grows. Existing methods attempt to capture this contextual information through attention selection or compression, but remain limited by bounded representations and lack explicit attention-level supervision to retain historical contributions to current queries. To address this, we introduce Attn-Forcing, a novel framework that preserves full-context attention contributions for streaming video generation under bounded memory and computation. We achieve this by introducing attention proxies that continuously approximate the attention responses induced by the historical context. Specifically, we implement the proxies as learnable visual latents and employ a Proxy Update Module to incorporate visual context from historical latents. Moreover, we propose an Attention Matching Loss to explicitly constrain the attention behavior of the learned proxies using full-context attention supervision. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that Attn-Forcing consistently improves streaming video generation quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing baseline methods.

papers.title: Plausible but Unimplantable: A Trustworthiness Audit of Shape Completion Foundation Models for Cranial Defect Reconstruction
papers.summary: A patient who has lost part of the skull vault needs an implant that fits the defect exactly, and such implants are still drawn by hand in CAD by specialists, which makes each case slow and expensive. The task can be considered as a shape completion problem, so pretrained completion models, and now the first shape completion foundation models, look like a way to remove that manual step. We audited three publicly released pretrained shape completion models, two of them foundation models, applied zero-shot to 239 cranial defects, some carved from public skull datasets and some real post-craniectomy cases. Each output was compared with simply returning the patient's own remaining bone, and tested for whether the predicted material could be placed without intersecting the bone that is still there. On the 210 carved defects none of the three improved on doing nothing, and on the 29 real cases only one did so beyond chance. Yet not one output, from any model in any configuration, was implantable: none managed both to stay clear of the bone the patient still has and to place more material than doing nothing, where a task-specific volumetric model, trained for this task and selected on these cases, was implantable on all but one. The output that most convincingly resembles a skull is no more placeable than the rest, and at these point densities implant thickness cannot be read off the emitted points at all, which is a property of the output representation rather than of any one model. On this evidence the shape completion foundation models we could obtain cannot be trusted and, used as released, are not usable in clinical practice. Substantial research towards trustworthy foundation models for shape completion is still needed.

papers.title: Dual Effect and Certainty Equivalence Revisited for a Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
papers.summary: This paper revisits the relation between dual effect and certainty equivalence (CE) through a scalar linear-Gaussian model. In dual control, the current input affects not only the immediate cost but also the information available for future decisions, and hence the future cost. Dynamic programming (DP) provides a natural framework for formulating dual control problems. At each step of the Bellman recursion, an optimal input minimizes the sum of the stage cost and the expected cost-to-go. We restrict attention to stage costs minimized by the CE input. However, CE may not minimize the Bellman objective because of the input-dependent expected cost-to-go. Classical no-dualeffect (NDE) conditions guarantee CE optimality in certain problem classes by requiring the conditional distribution of the estimation error to be independent of past controls. In the present model, we observe that CE can remain optimal at the level of a single Bellman recursion even when the classical NDE conditions fail, provided that the expected cost-to-go is independent of the current input. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a notion of NDE formulated directly at the level of the Bellman objective, which we call Bellman-side NDE. Under some mild regularity conditions, we show that Bellman-side NDE can be characterized by a heat equation. This characterization identifies the class of Bellman-side NDE functions, and further yields a decomposition of a generic cost-to-go function into a Bellman-side NDE component and a dual-effect component.

papers.title: Measurement-Guided Conversion of Laboratory Eye-Tracking Data for VR Authentication
papers.summary: Eye-movement authentication in virtual reality (VR) needs longitudinal training data, yet most such datasets come from lab trackers. We convert lab recordings to a VR headset's signal quality while keeping their eye movement, using only unpaired VR recordings of other people. Measurements show that the headset's added noise dominates above 7.8 Hz and that its quality is consistent within a person. A parametric device model re-creates the headset's sampling, a person-consistent calibration error and spectrally shaped noise, and a frequency-locked diffusion renderer re-textures that high-frequency noise. Converted GazeBase recordings match GazeBaseVR in noise level and accuracy, keep their source's saccade dynamics, and are harder to tell from real VR data than two prior conversions. An authenticator trained only on converted data verifies unseen VR users at a 5.9% equal error rate with 45 s of gaze, close to real VR training (5.8%); with 5 s, a gap remains.

papers.title: Modeling QNMs-Filtered Gravitational Waveforms: Approximation Limits and Filtering Effects
papers.summary: The waveform left after quasinormal modes filtering of binary gravitational waveforms, often called the direct wave, has recently attracted considerable debate. Analytic models of this residual waveform involve several levels of approximation, while the effects of filtering on the modeling remain unclear. These issues require further investigation. In this paper, we examine the approximation errors, limits of applicability, and role of filtering in these models. We find that the point-particle models examined here show notable discrepancies with the filtered Binary-black-holes waveforms. Analytic particle templates based on the stationary-phase approximation perform reasonably well for the \((\ell,m)=(2,2)\) multipole, but exhibit substantial limitations for the \((4,4)\). Although the filter is all-pass, it substantially affects the modeling results. Our analytic calculations on a Schwarzschild background further show that vacuum perturbations with Gaussian initial data can also exhibit direct-wave-like waveforms after filtering, with their morphology depending on the location of the initial data relative to the light ring.

papers.title: Methane and ethane adsorption on calcite surfaces: effects of surface morphology from molecular dynamics and 3D-RISM
papers.summary: Understanding the adsorption of alkanes on mineral surfaces is important for industrial processes such as oil and gas recovery from shale reservoirs. Previous studies have examined the adsorption of functionalized and non-functionalized alkanes on calcite, as well as adsorption under confinement. However, real surfaces commonly exhibit defects that can influence adsorption behavior. In this work, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the three-dimensional reference interaction site model (3D-RISM) are used to investigate the adsorption of methane and ethane on calcite surfaces with step defects. MD simulations were carried out with and without positional restraints to investigate the effects of carbonate reorientation. 3D-RISM calculations were performed on these structures and on energy-minimized configurations of the relaxed crystal. Both methods show adsorption enhanced at step defects relative to flat regions, with methane exhibiting higher excess adsorption than ethane. Carbonate reorientation at the relaxed step edges reduces the local density peaks at specific step sites in both methods, while the integrated excess adsorption from MD remains comparable to that of the restrained surface. 3D-RISM predicts lower maxima for the highest density peaks and larger excess adsorption than MD, but reproduces the spatial organization and overall adsorption trends at a fraction of the computational cost. These results highlight the importance of surface heterogeneity in fluid-mineral interactions and demonstrate that 3D-RISM is an efficient tool for semi-quantitative screening of adsorption across complex surface geometries

papers.title: Relation of Rotation and Pulsation Properties in $γ$ Doradus Stars
papers.summary: Connection between stellar rotation and pulsation amplitude has been proposed for several types of pulsating variable stars, but no such relation has been established for gamma Doradus stars from spectroscopic v sin i measurements. A high-amplitude gamma Dor subclass was also suggested recently, which had not been explored by spectroscopic means before. We investigate the connection between rotation and pulsational properties of gamma Dor stars using a homogeneous spectroscopic sample with available TESS light curves. We obtained new stellar spectra with the ACE spectrograph on the 1-m RCC telescope of Konkoly Observatory and measured v sin i for a sample of 124 targets. For target selection, Gaia classifications were combined with TESS photometry. We used Fourier methods to determine the dominant frequencies from all available TESS light curves through sector 98. We also performed rotation- and inclination-dependent mode visibility modelling relying on GYRE Hough functions with TAR visibilities for the interpretation of our results. We find a decreasing upper envelope in both the peak-to-peak amplitude and the dominant-component semi-amplitude as a function of v sin i: high-v sin i stars show only low photometric amplitudes, whereas high-amplitude stars have low v sin i. We also confirm a positive relation between v sin i and the dominant pulsation frequency. The highest observed amplitudes also decrease towards higher dominant frequencies. Visibility modelling indicates that these trends cannot be explained by geometric effects alone, suggesting that the intrinsic pulsation amplitudes of gamma Dor stars physically decrease with increasing equatorial rotational velocity. Furthermore, the strong suppression of zonal dipole mode visibility at high rotation suggests that high-amplitude gamma Dor stars are likely slow rotators or moderate rotators viewed nearly pole-on.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics. 9 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables available also on CDS. Further electronic materials are available at: https://hdl.handle.net/21.15109/ARP/ZW1ZLV

papers.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science
papers.summary: The Pandora spacecraft is a smallsat selected in NASA's inaugural class of Pioneers missions. The aim of the Pandora mission is to disentangle stellar activity signals from exoplanet atmospheric transmission spectroscopy measurements. Pandora accomplishes this goal with its combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy that observe each target in the prime mission for 10 separate transit observations, each spanning 24 hours at a time. Targets were carefully selected for the Pandora prime mission. Pandora is specifically studying planets around low-mass stellar hosts (K and M dwarf stars) spanning a range of rotation periods and activity levels. The planets range in size from 1.5 - 15 Earth radii and orbital periods ranging from 1.7 - 11.5 days. In addition to the 10 transit visits planned for each of the 20 prime mission targets, Pandora is observing a number of auxiliary targets encompassing a variety of science topics. This includes topics such as stellar activity and young systems, transit timing variations of exoplanets, brown dwarf compositions, exoplanet phase curves, etc. We will discuss the selection of these targets, how they have been scheduled to fill in gaps in prime mission operations, and early science results. If the mission is extended, there is further opportunity for accomplishing additional science. Here we will discuss the possible options for extended mission operations and science.
papers.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 1 table; paper published as proceedings of the SPIE

papers.title: The recent counterexamples to the Eisenbud-Schreyer-Weyman Ulrich problem (2003) and to Hochster's small Cohen-Macaulay conjecture (1973): a survey, with a generalization to arbitrary dimension
papers.summary: In September 2026 four preprints and an AI-generated manuscript moved one numerical obstruction from projective geometry to local algebra. For a smooth complex projective surface $Y$ with an ample, globally generated divisor $H$ such that $H^2<σ(Y)$, the signature, one obtains in turn: no Ulrich bundles when $H$ is very ample (Anghel, arXiv:2609.02718; extended to every dimension by Lopez, arXiv:2609.06678), answering negatively the Eisenbud-Schreyer-Weyman question of 2003 for sheaves supported on the whole variety; no arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay bundles, i.e. section rings without graded maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules in characteristic zero (Anghel, arXiv:2609.15589); and complete local domains without small Cohen-Macaulay modules, counterexamples to Hochster's 1973 conjecture, if $K_Y\equiv4H$ (Chen, arXiv:2609.24142, proposed) or $σ>2H^2$ (OpenAI, released 6 October). We recall the definitions and main statements, and add two things. First, through a finite projection to $\mathbb P^2$ and an identity already present in the OpenAI manuscript, the three obstructions become one variance identity; for surfaces this explains the factor $2$ between the graded bound $σ\le H^2$ and the local $σ\le2H^2$. Second, we generalize the argument of the OpenAI manuscript to every dimension $m\ge2$, with complete proofs: if $X$ is a smooth complex projective variety of dimension $m$ and $H$ an ample, globally generated divisor, a small Cohen-Macaulay module over the completed section ring of $(X,H)$ forces $(K_X^2-2c_2(X))\cdot H^{m-2}\le(m+4)H^m$. Consequently the completed section rings of all Hesse pairs, including the ball quotient of the first preprint, have no small Cohen-Macaulay module, and products of Hesse surfaces with projective spaces give complete local domains with an isolated singularity, of every dimension $\ge3$, without small Cohen-Macaulay modules.
papers.comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Survey; Sections 9 and 10 contain new results with complete proofs

papers.title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
papers.summary: Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens - and that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. We show that one layer is lost by every mainstream converter - the meaning an author encodes in how text looks - and that the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete. We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out, scored against the file's own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 0.690 to 0.150 (docling) and 0.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors - five Claude models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI's GPT-5.6. An agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling's false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag is four times ours. A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues - highlight (+0.302) and colour (+0.262), both Holm-adjusted p < 1e-4 - while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each sit within +/-0.003 of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: 32.8% of 6,460 documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, 10.3% on an obligation. A pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085 beyond merely preserving it (Holm-adjusted p = 0.049). We validate the labels against rendered page images through an independent modality (kappa = 0.72) and bound what wording alone can achieve (AUC 0.664). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.

papers.title: Zeros of $E_2$, quasi-periods, and Schwarz maps
papers.summary: We study the zeros of the Eisenstein series $E_2$, their distribution near rational cusps, and the values of modular functions at these zeros. Using Watson's inversion formula, we prove that the number of zeros in $0\leq\operatorname{Re}τ<1$ with imaginary part at least $Y$ satisfies \[ N(Y)=\frac{1}{2πY} +O\!\left(Y^{-1/2}\log\frac1Y\right) \qquad(Y\to0^+). \] We also determine the limiting distribution of the scaled displacements from the cusps and prove that two zeros whose difference is rational differ by an integer. At every zero $ρ$, classical transcendence theorems imply that both $j(ρ)$ and $λ(ρ)$ are transcendental. We use this fact to obtain an exact multiplicity formula for arithmetic quasimodular forms at arbitrary congruence level and to show that all ordinary derivatives of arithmetic modular functions on congruence subgroups, evaluated at $ρ$, are algebraic over $\overline{\mathbb Q}(j(ρ),j'(ρ))$. We then relate Watson's formula to the Schwarz map of a rational transform of the Legendre hypergeometric equation. Finally, we give conditional results on the transcendence of $ρ$ under modular Schanuel and period conjectures, and determine why the associated analytic subgroup fails the rank condition in Waldschmidt's theorem.

papers.title: Tempered Langevin diffusions with polynomial-tailed targets: explosions, moment thresholds and ergodicity
papers.summary: For tempered Langevin diffusions (TLDs) targeting polynomially tailed measures, the convergence rate is known to change from polynomial to exponential to uniform as the temperature rises through a critical value. We explain this transition by the tails of the marginal laws of the norm of the TLD, up to a second, larger critical temperature beyond which the TLD explodes. As the temperature increases, these tails change from stretched-exponential, through super-polynomial at the first critical temperature, to polynomial, mirroring the transition in the convergence rate. Moreover, this tail analysis gives a complete quantification of the convergence rates throughout the non-explosive regime, in both $f$-variation and Wasserstein distances.
papers.comment: 24 pages; for short YouTube presentation discussing the main results, see https://youtu.be/P0yIqm6K5r0, and proofs, see https://youtu.be/ygnPmOUINWM

papers.title: RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures
papers.summary: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
papers.comment: 19 pages, 11 figures, including supplementary material. To appear in SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/realme

papers.title: Stationarity Constraints Improve Both Energies and Densities of Machine-Learned Exchange-Correlation Functionals
papers.summary: Empirical exchange-correlation functionals are fitted on fixed orbitals but used self-consistently, so better energies often come with worse densities. We show that the Brillouin residual of a trained functional on the Kohn-Sham orbitals of an accurate density controls, to first order, both the self-consistent density shift and the gap between fitted and self-consistent energies. Penalizing it requires no self-consistent-field solution during training. Trained on 6 energies and 11 CCSD densities, a neural meta-GGA surpasses SCAN in both atomization energies and densities of unseen molecules.

papers.title: On the gap of thresholds
papers.summary: We propose an algorithm to compute the gap numbers of log canonical thresholds, anticanonical thresholds, and $\mathbb{R}$-complementary thresholds for surface pairs with a given rational hyperstandard coefficient set. As an example, we compute these gap numbers for a special hyperstandard set that appears in the effective boundedness of $n$-complements for surface pairs.

papers.title: CAQ: Clustered Asymptotically Anytime-Valid Quantile Treatment Effects for Online Experiments
papers.summary: Confidence sequences let an experiment be monitored continuously without inflating error, but the existing constructions for quantiles assume that observations arrive independently. In online experiments this rarely holds: randomization assigns users, while the metric is computed over the many correlated events each user generates, so intervals built for independent data are too narrow and miss the truth more often than their nominal rate allows. We propose CAQ, a confidence sequence for a quantile that is both robust to this within-user dependence and valid at arbitrary stopping times, together with a sequential test for the difference in a quantile between two treatment arms. The width adapts to the dependence actually present, widening beyond the independent-data benchmark only when correlation within users is strong. In simulations, CAQ is the only method we tested that holds both coverage and false-positive rate at their nominal levels across clustering strengths and heavy-tailed data, while the fixed-horizon baseline fails under continuous monitoring and the independence-assuming sequential baseline fails as within-user correlation grows.
papers.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables, 2 algorithms. Accepted at the Conference on Digital Experimentation at MIT (CODE@MIT) 2026

papers.title: ExGrad: Beyond Suppression - Explicit Clean-Gradient Subtraction in Adversarial Training
papers.summary: Adversarial training derives updates from surrogate losses, but source-loss descent does not directly characterize an update's effect on adversarial margins. We introduce ExGrad (extrapolative gradient recomposition), which constructs clean-input, adversarial-input, and adversarial-weight-perturbed (AWP) gradients. Virtual steps measure their margin responses, and a globally solvable three-variable problem selects coefficients over a bounded affine domain without nonnegativity constraints. Across affine radii on CIFAR-10, negative clean coefficients rapidly predominate and increase in magnitude with the radius. Cross-zero interventions show that setting the clean coefficient to zero is insufficient: mild subtraction improves PGD-20, while stronger subtraction trades clean accuracy for further PGD-20 gains. In CIFAR-10 WRN-28-4 controls, none of the three candidate-removal variants matches full ExGrad. Projection diagnostics show that negative clean coefficients usually coexist with positive net clean-axis projections, although both decrease as the radius grows. Norm-matched controls indicate that update magnitude alone does not explain the moderate-radius gains. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 show radius-dependent improvements over AWP. On CIFAR-100, ExGrad at $R=0.8$ improves all five reported metrics, including clean and AutoAttack accuracy by 3.84 and 1.75 percentage points. On ImageNet-100, the same radius improves all four robust metrics over both AWP and PGD-AT. These results identify clean-gradient subtraction as a response-revealed update preference whose strength and clean-robust operating point are controlled by the affine radius.

papers.title: GuideEvolve: Self-Evolving Agent Framework with Expert Guidance and 3Ts Mechanisms
papers.summary: This study introduces GuideEvolve, a self-evolving agent framework incorporating expert guidance and three autonomous regulatory mechanisms, collectively termed the 3Ts: Think Fast and Slow, Throwback, and Termination by choice. The framework addresses critical limitations in extant self-evolving agent paradigms through dual innovations: (1) a task-specific expert-evaluation-driven evolutionary pipeline, and (2) the integration of 3Ts mechanisms to facilitate cognitive optimization, performance recovery via temporal rollback, and adaptive termination protocols. Empirical validation across the MGSM and MMLU benchmarks demonstrates that GuideEvolve attains performance metrics comparable to current state-of-the-art models (89.8% accuracy versus Gödel Agent's 90.6% on MGSM; 89.1% versus 87.9% on MMLU), while exhibiting notably reduced variance (25-59%) and enhanced robustness. Furthermore, the framework achieves a 100% evolution success rate, superior to the baseline's 82%, diminishes required optimization iterations by approximately 50% (from 30 iterations in baseline to 15.1 and 13.4 across tasks), and provides improved stability for production deployment.

papers.title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
papers.summary: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings.
