Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.
papers.comment: Full paper accepted and presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik (WI 2025), Münster, Germany. To appear in the conference proceedings (Lecture Notes in Information Systems and Organisation, Springer). This version is the submitted manuscript prior to peer review

papers.title: RECAP: Representation-Based Calibration with Amortized Pooling for Frequentist Simulation-Based Inference
papers.summary: Simulation-based inference enables uncertainty quantification in broad contexts when a simulation model is available but when a test statistic's sampling distribution is not tractable. But, frequentist calibration in this setting can be costly over high-dimensional parameter spaces. In this paper, we introduce RECAP (REpresentation-based Calibration with Amortized Pooling), a general framework for frequentist simulation-based inference. RECAP exploits low-dimensional structure in how the null distribution varies with parameters and is particularly useful when the parameter dimension is high or when different parameter configurations have redundant or compensating effects. RECAP pools simulated scores according to a representation that preserves this distribution exactly or approximately, allowing distant parameter values to share calibration information. Representations may be derived from model structure or learned independently. Empirical quantiles of the pooled scores then yield tests and confidence sets, for which we establish theoretical coverage guarantees. In the simulation studies, we show that RECAP has lower coverage error than existing approaches and power close to that of the point-wise oracle, while maintaining the computational benefits of amortized calibration. An application to population genomics illustrates learned low-dimensional calibration and interpretable uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Real-Time 24-hour Ahead Forecasting of Solar Energetic Particle Events with SEPNET-PRISM-R
papers.summary: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events, operationally defined as proton flux exceeding 10 pfu in the >10 MeV channel, threaten spacecraft systems, astronaut safety, and high latitude aviation, yet continuous real-time forecasting with adequate lead time remains difficult. We present SEPNET-PRISM-R, a near-real-time system that issues hourly, 24 hour ahead probabilistic SEP forecasts. The model integrates multimodal solar data - including active region patches, flare features, coronal mass ejection (CME) characteristics, and historical proton flux - to concurrently predict SEP occurrences, peak proton flux, soft X-ray flux, and CME velocity, with the primary objective being SEP forecasting. Building on existing literature, SEPNET-PRISM-R enhances operational performance by incorporating a postprocessing module that enables cross-validated decision making and interpretable quantification of feature importance. The training dataset spans from February 1986 to September 2025, with subsequent forecasts generated sequentially through the present via a real-time space weather prediction platform that provides predictive probabilities, feature attributions, and historical analogs, enabling more reliable and informed operational decision-making. The proposed framework substantially suppresses false alarm rates while maintaining robust event detection capabilities, as evidenced by case studies and aggregate statistics.

papers.title: Diversity, Efficiency, and Incentives in Political Prediction Markets
papers.summary: Critics of political prediction markets argue that prices are biased because traders are not representative of voters. We test this claim by analyzing data from political betting markets spanning more than 100 years. Our analysis yields two main findings: (1) Acros markets, traders were not representative of the voters. (2) Prices were not biased by political preferences of participants. For the 2024 election, we analyzed anonymized data from Kalshi, a CFTC-regulated exchange, the largest regulated political prediction market in the U.S. Kalshi's traders were 86% male and half were under 30. In its first month of listing election contracts, Kalshi's prices were more accurate than every poll-based forecast in the national race, the seven battleground states, and nineteen Senate races, and no poll-based forecast would have been profitable to trade against them in any group of presidential contests. Its volume came from areas that voted 28% Republican, while 60% of volume went to Republican positions. Traders with a single trade placed 73% of their volume on Harris. The association between a trader's location and the direction of positions declines with trading activity and is zero among active traders, who account for most of the volume. Prices can be accurate with unrepresentative traders when the forecasts of profit-motivated traders do not depend on their demographics. Two other markets corroborate our findings. In New York's 1900 market, bettors were older than the population and drawn from finance. On PredictIt in 2016, which limited each trader to $850 per contract, positions followed registered party more closely, as our theory predicts when market restrictions do not allow profit-motivated traders to set the price. Prediction market efficiency is driven by financial incentives over demographic representativeness.

papers.title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

papers.title: Composite Variable Strategies for Continuous Endpoints
papers.summary: Composite endpoints are common in clinical trials for binary, time-to-event or recurrent outcomes. Recently, there has been interest in estimands for continuous endpoints that employ a composite variable strategy for handling intercurrent events, whereby a value on the continuous scale is defined as the outcome. In this paper we describe these continuous composite endpoints where participants who experience the intercurrent event are assigned a pre-specified value on the outcome scale (which we call the failure value) instead of a measurement. We describe these endpoints and the difficulty of choosing the failure value when the mean is the chosen summary statistic. The large impact of the choice of failure value on the variance of the distribution of the endpoint is quantified as a function of the probability of the event and the standardised difference of the failure value from the mean of the unaffected values. Strategies for choosing failure values are discussed, emphasising the need to balance the clinical relevance and interpretability of the estimand with the need to reliably estimate it. Two potential solutions to situations where there is no relevant and viable choice of failure value are proposed; using failure values based on distributional characteristics to generate clinical relevance and using alternative summary measures to avoid the need to select specific values.

papers.title: Reconciling anomalous quadrupole deformation in $^{200,202}$Hg with Coulomb excitation
papers.summary: Stable isotopes of mercury, with two fewer protons than magic lead, are found experimentally to exhibit oblate deformation, similar to neighbouring platinum isotopes. These isotopes are of special interest due to the use of $^{199}$Hg as an experimental laboratory for electric dipole moment searches, which are a powerful test of charge-parity ($CP$) violation and the interpretation of which depends critically on the quadrupole and octopule shapes of the underlying nucleus. It is observed that the ratio between experimental quadrupole moments and electric quadrupole transition strengths exceed physical limits, placing uncertainty on this underlying shape. In an effort to resolve this situation, a Coulomb excitation experiment was performed to remeasure the spectroscopic quadrupole moment ($Q_s(2^+_1)$) of $^{200}$Hg and $^{202}$Hg utilising $^{48}$Ti and $^{120}$Sn targets. The values obtained were $Q_s(2^+_1)$ $^{200,202}$Hg = $0.52(14)$, $0.63(10)$ eb, lying within physical limits defined by $B(E2)$ values but still consistent with near axially-symmetric oblate deformation. A systematic study of nuclei indicates that, as with neighbouring Pt isotopes, $^{200,202}$Hg are strongly oblate deformed, albeit without fully developing into an axial rotor.

papers.title: The Scale of Universalization in Multiplicative Kantian Equilibrium
papers.summary: Multiplicative Kantian equilibrium requires agents to evaluate whether they would prefer all players to change their actions by a common proportional factor. This note argues that such a counterfactual is not fully specified by the material payoff environment alone: one must also specify the scale in which proportional universalization is performed. Building on the Sher-Roemer discussion of strategic non-invariance, we characterize how a smooth monotone reparametrization of actions changes the multiplicative Kantian first-order condition. We then illustrate the issue in a simple two-country abatement problem. Universalizing physical abatement and universalizing abatement expenditures are both natural interpretations of "doing one's part," but they lead to different Kantian outcomes, even though they describe the same material environment. The note also identifies special cases in which the interior first-order condition is representation-invariant, including common-exponent power transformations and symmetric profiles under identical transformations. The conclusion is constructive: applying multiplicative Kantian equilibrium to an economic environment requires specifying both the use of the Kantian criterion and the represented scale in which the Kantian counterfactual is evaluated.

papers.title: Where Has the Foreign Signal Gone?
papers.summary: We compare the relation between sentiment noise in the Twitter feed and losses for stocks of domestic and foreign firms. The mean quarterly domestic-foreign difference in the slope of next-quarter losses on measured noise is -1.40 (Newey-West t = -2.99). This slope is negative for 78 and 48 percent of the quarters for domestic and foreign stocks, respectively (block-bootstrap p = 0.016). Thus, this relationship is temporally more stable for domestic stocks. We use a noisy rational expectations model to explain these patterns through the composition of the contributor pool. The feeds for stocks of foreign firms have higher repeat-author concentration and a larger model-implied nonfundamental component than those for domestic firms. We interpret these differences through the producer-knowledge mismatch hypothesis. For foreign firms, the English-language contributor pool underrepresents the home-market investors who tend to possess informational advantages about them. Thus, the foreign signal is not gone but diluted.

papers.title: An exact coexistence criterion for stochastic Lotka--Volterra systems with Volterra--Lyapunov stable interactions
papers.summary: We consider stochastic Lotka-Volterra systems $dX=\mathrm{Diag}(X)(α+AX)dt+\mathrm{Diag}(X)ΓdB$ with nondegenerate noise and a Volterra-Lyapunov stable interaction matrix $A$, that is, $DA+A^\top D\prec 0$ for some positive diagonal matrix $D$. This class covers every self-limited predator-prey food web that is conservative in the sense of Volterra, in particular every such web whose interaction graph is a forest. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for invariant coexistence: the process has an invariant probability measure on $(0,\infty)^n$, that is, a stationary distribution under which all species have positive densities, if and only if $m=-A^{-1}β$ is positive, where $β=α-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{diag}(ΓΓ^\top)$ is the vector of noise-corrected growth rates. This measure is then unique and ergodic, has mean $m$, and attracts every interior initial condition exponentially fast in total variation. Thus environmental noise affects coexistence only through the Itô shift $α\mapstoβ$, and the criterion is the exact counterpart of the feasibility criterion for the deterministic system $\dot x=\mathrm{Diag}(x)(β+Ax)$. Both directions rest on the fact that, for Lotka-Volterra systems, invasion rates are affine in the mean of the underlying measure. Necessity follows from an exact formula for the means of invariant measures supported on faces of the orthant. Sufficiency follows from the persistence theorem of Hening and Nguyen, for which the explicit weights $Dm$ give a stochastic counterpart of Hofbauer's average Lyapunov function, so that no enumeration of the invariant measures on the boundary is required. Applied to subcommunities, the result also characterizes every stationary regime in which some species are absent.

papers.title: Ab initio-guided optical potentials for semi-magic nuclei from Gorkov self-consistent Green's functions
papers.summary: We construct ab initio-guided nonlocal optical potentials for semi-magic nuclei from the self-consistent Gorkov-ADC(2) one-body Green's function. This extends ab initio self-consistent Green's function approaches to open-shell targets and to proton projectiles. The starting point is the NNLO$_{\rm sat}$ chiral interaction, whose three-nucleon component is included as an effective two-body interaction. The self-energy is computed in a harmonic-oscillator basis, transformed to coordinate space and used in the scattering code SIDES. Its imaginary part relies on a phenomenological energy-dependent width, hence the label ab initio-guided. Differential and integral (total and reaction) cross sections are compared with data for n,p+$^{40}$Ca and p+$^{42}$Ca. Forward angles are well reproduced. Backward angles reveal a lack of absorption, which calls for larger model spaces and many-body truncations beyond Gorkov-ADC(2).
papers.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to the proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Nuclear Reaction Mechanisms, Varenna (Italy), 2026

papers.title: A multiplier bootstrap score test for Tobit specification
papers.summary: In this paper, we propose a simple score-based specification test for the Tobit regression model, implemented through a computationally efficient multiplier bootstrap. We test correct specification through the conditional moment restriction that the generalized Tobit residual has zero conditional mean, and construct a feasible score-based empirical process using the integrated conditional moments approach, conditioning on the estimated index so that no smoothing or tuning parameter is required. We derive a first-order uniform representation of the feasible process, showing how its limiting behavior is affected by maximum-likelihood estimation of the structural parameter, and obtain the asymptotic properties of the corresponding Kolmogorov--Smirnov statistic under the null, fixed alternatives, and a sequence of local alternatives. Since the limiting null distribution is non-pivotal, $p$-values are obtained from a multiplier bootstrap that mimics the first-order representation and therefore captures the parameter estimation uncertainty. Monte Carlo experiments, including an unknown-scale design, an index-visible/index-invisible power study, and comparisons with existing specification tests, confirm accurate size and competitive power across a range of designs and covariate dimensions. Two empirical applications further demonstrate the practical utility of our approach.

papers.title: Digital Nudge Effects in Optimal Stopping Games: Antagonistic Interactions in Layered Choice Architectures
papers.summary: Digital nudges have become a prominent area of research in human-centered interaction, yet little is known about how they interact when deployed together. This study examines the individual and combined effects of anchoring, salience, and social proof digital nudges on stopping behavior and outcome quality in a sequential decision task. Using a 2^3 between-subjects factorial design grounded in the secretary problem (N = 181), we find that (1) an anchor nudge significantly increased exploration rather than constraining it (b = 1.207, p = .017); (2) the salience nudge produced the smallest effect of any condition; and (3) combining the anchor and social proof nudges produced the worst outcome quality of any condition ($181.83 vs. $192.21 for anchor-only), with outcome quality declining monotonically as nudge count increased. These findings provide the first controlled evidence for a digital nudge crowding-out effect with direct implications for the ethical design of digital interfaces.

papers.title: Occupational Uniqueness and Wage Growth
papers.summary: Changes in occupational task content may have different economic implications depending on whether the tasks gained or lost are occupation-specific or already widespread across the economy. Existing measures of occupational task change largely abstract from this distinction, treating occupations as self-contained task bundles rather than accounting for how tasks are distributed across occupations. We develop a framework to measure a distinct dimension of occupational change, one that goes beyond task expertise or task content: task structure. Using this new framework that tracks tasks across occupations and over time, we separate changes in task quantity from changes in occupational uniqueness, defined as the distinctiveness of an occupation's task bundle relative to other occupations. Using a harmonized dataset of 196563 task statements from the Dictionary of Occupational Titles and O*NET spanning 1977-2018, we measure task diffusion, occupational uniqueness, and distinct dimensions of task addition and removal. Occupations that become less unique are also associated with lower wage growth, and the wage associations of task additions and removals depend on how widely the affected tasks are performed elsewhere. Adding highly diffused tasks is associated with lower wage growth, as is removing occupation-specific tasks. At the economy-wide dimension, however, the pattern differs: the addition of new tasks is positively associated with wage growth, whereas the removal of tasks is negatively associated with it. Taken together, these results show that similar changes in the number of tasks performed by an occupation can reflect economically distinct processes. Incorporating the cross-occupational distribution of tasks, therefore, provides a richer account of occupational change and its relationship to the wage structure.

papers.title: Speculative Imbalance Positions by Non-Physical Traders: Impacts on Electricity System Balancing in Great Britain
papers.summary: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.

papers.title: Arithmetic Models for Commodity Futures, Vanilla, and Calendar Spread Options
papers.summary: We develop an arithmetic multi-factor stochastic volatility model for commodity futures and options. The arithmetic specification yields a low-dimensional Markovian representation of the futures curve and semi-closed-form pricing formulas for vanilla and basket options, including calendar spread options. These properties make the model suitable for large-scale empirical estimation. We estimate the model using an unscented Kalman filter on a panel of WTI crude oil futures, vanilla options, and calendar spread options spanning 2013-2024. We find that three stochastic volatility factors are needed to capture both the level and slope of the volatility term structure, and that hedges based on these factors remove almost all of the daily risk of a portfolio of vanilla options. Calendar spread options provide information about the dependence structure of futures prices that is not captured by futures and vanilla options alone. A model estimated without calendar spread options systematically overprices them by overstating the decorrelation between adjacent futures contracts. Including these options in the estimation brings the model's decorrelation close to the observed decorrelation, which removes the overpricing and improves their hedges, at only a small loss of accuracy in the pricing and hedging of vanilla options. Finally, we show that the arithmetic model fits futures and vanilla options better than its geometric counterpart and hedges the vanilla options slightly better.

papers.title: Deciphering Entangled Fission at Finite Excitations via Thermal Subspace Projection
papers.summary: The sharing of particles and energy between entangled fission fragments is known to contribute considerably to final observable distributions. This work unravels this sharing mechanism at finite excitations, which exhibits an intriguing quantum-thermal interplay relevant to long-standing open questions in induced fission. We formulate a thermal double particle-number projection onto spatial subspaces, using the Balian-Brezin representation and Grassmann integrals, to derive the projected partition function and observables. Based on finite-temperature dynamical fission calculations of 240Pu, the formalism explains the puzzling energy dependence of odd-even staggering in charge yields and of sawtooth neutron multiplicities. The present framework also provides a general projection tool for probing entangled thermal many-body systems.

papers.title: Direct Urca process facilitated by non-Fermi-liquid quantum criticality
papers.summary: Conventional Fermi-liquid theories of dense nuclear matter predict that the direct Urca process requires a proton fraction above a threshold of $Y_p \approx 0.11$--$0.15$, which is rarely reached in low-mass neutron stars. Here we show that this stringent kinematic constraint is drastically relaxed by the non-Fermi liquid behavior arising from superfluid and superconducting quantum criticality in neutron stars. In the non-Fermi-liquid regimes, nucleons have a smooth momentum occupation without a sharp Fermi surface, and their chemical potentials develop a logarithmic temperature dependence. These intrinsic features fundamentally alter the standard $β$-equilibrium relation. Consequently, direct Urca neutrino emission can be activated even at low nuclear densities. This modifies the long-standing Urca-threshold paradigm and indicates that direct Urca process has the opportunity to occur in low-mass neutron stars.

papers.title: System-evolutionary view of RNA presence in living cells
papers.summary: Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA-DNA-Protein network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction-survival axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA-primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these have contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where RNA did not lose in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy and in its various forms has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.
papers.journal: Segerståhl and Jalasvuori (2026) System-Evolutionary View of RNA Presence in Living Cells. In G. Witzany (Ed.), Integrative Theory of Evolution - Aspects and Insights. Springer, Cham. pp. 357-377

papers.title: Understanding CEO-Employee compensation dynamics: An agent-based simulation approach
papers.summary: CEO compensation has often been examined from the top down, i.e., as the outcome of a negotiation between the CEO, the board of directors, and the shareholders. While these approaches have provided valuable insights into the nature of CEO compensation and its relations with firm performance and intra-firm inequality, we believe they leave aside the internal decision-making dynamics of CEOs and employees. To fill this research gap, we develop an agent-based model built on the NK framework in which a CEO compensated for long-term firm performance interacts with several employees rewarded for short-term departmental performance. This temporal dichotomy in their respective compensation functions creates a potential temporal misalignment of incentives. By varying the horizon considered by the CEO to make their decisions, we examine how this temporal (mis)alignment of incentives shapes firm performance and pay inequality between the CEO and the employees. Our findings suggest that aligning the CEO's horizon with the employees' short-term incentives yields the highest performance, raising both the level attained and the speed of improvement across all task environments examined. This finding contrasts with the usual advice given in CEO compensation research, which is to avoid short-termism. Furthermore, the model shows that the longest horizon examined produces both the lowest performance and the highest pay inequality. This pattern, commonly attributed to managerial power, emerges in our model from incentive misalignment alone, without agents holding any power over their own compensation.

papers.title: From Harmonic Oscillators to Multiplicity Distributions in Particle Production Processes
papers.summary: We propose an oscillator framework of studying multi-particle production processes using the information theory approach. For a system of degenerate oscillators, we derive the negative binomial distribution (NBD) and its nonadditive generalization represented as gNBD. We observe that gNBD derived from nonadditive statistics describes data in higher multiplicity region, thereby providing an alternative for the multi-component distributions used in phenomenological studies. We also generalize our framework for non-degenerate oscillators and encounter a Lerch-type generalization of the Barnes zeta function that, to the best of our knowledge, has not been studied in the context of nonadditive statistics and multiplicity studies before.

papers.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
papers.summary: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/

papers.title: Peripheral nucleon-nucleon scattering with explicit vector mesons in chiral perturbation theory
papers.summary: Background: In chiral perturbation theory (ChPT), heavy degrees of freedom are integrated out, with their contributions absorbed into low-energy constants. Keeping the $ρ$ and $ω$ explicit within ChPT retains the finite-range momentum dependence associated with these mesons. Purpose: We study how explicit $ρ$ and $ω$ mesons affect peripheral $NN$ phase shifts. Methods: We incorporate the vector mesons by counting their masses as hard and the momentum they carry as soft. The next-to-next-to-leading-order nuclear force includes, in addition to one- and two-pion exchange, one-vector-meson exchange with dressed propagators and vertex functions. The vector propagators and vertex functions are fixed from the mesonic sector and the nucleon electromagnetic form factors. We calculate neutron--proton scattering with $J=3$--$5$ up to $T_{\rm lab}=300$ MeV and examine the sensitivity to one-pion-exchange iteration and the spectral-function regularization scheme. Results: The vector-meson contribution falls rapidly with $J$. In several $J=3$ waves it moves the phase shifts toward PWA93, while in other waves the change is small or moves the phase shift away. In ${}^{3}\mathrm{G}_{3}$ the change toward PWA93 persists under variations of the spectral cutoff, and its size is nearly independent of the treatment of one-pion exchange. The ${}^{3}\mathrm{D}_{3}$ wave is strongly cutoff dependent, and there the $ω$ contribution outweighs the opposing $ρ$ contribution. The tensor and spin-spin components of the $ρ$ interaction play the dominant roles in moving $ε_3$ and ${}^{1}\mathrm{F}_{3}$ toward PWA93, respectively. Conclusions: The effect of the explicit vector mesons on the peripheral phase shifts is channel dependent. The $ρ$ meson gives the dominant shifts toward PWA93, particularly in $ε_3$ and ${}^{3}\mathrm{G}_{3}$.

papers.title: VISH-ASR: Viterbi-Guided Selection of Hotwords for Speech-LLM Contextual ASR
papers.summary: Prompt-based contextual ASR requires selecting a compact hotword subset from large dynamic inventories, yet existing pre-selection methods rely either on discrete ASR hypotheses that may discard acoustic evidence or on separately trained retrieval models. We propose Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords (VISH), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that directly verifies candidate-specific acoustic support over frame-level CTC posteriors. VISH formulates pre-selection as constrained posterior search; M-VISH makes large-list verification scalable through frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search with bounded top-K pruning, while Bi-MVISH exploits complementary backward evidence for robust verification. Across five benchmarks, M-VISH achieves up to 11.7% absolute improvement in Best-F1 over a strong learned-retrieval baseline and reduces candidate-search latency by 75.2% at 2,000 candidates relative to hypothesis-based filtering. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of posterior-level verification for accurate and scalable hotword pre-selection without additional model training.

papers.title: Central Limit Theorems for Optimal Transport Functionals
papers.summary: We establish central limit theorems for empirical plug-in estimators of scalar functionals of quadratic optimal transport maps and potentials, including Wasserstein costs and several risk measures constructed from transport-based multivariate quantiles. We study the one-sample problem with a known reference distribution and i.i.d. observations from the target distribution. A natural approach is to combine a limit theorem for the empirical transport map with the functional delta method. We show, however, that in dimensions at least two, empirical transport-map errors admit no nonzero weak limit in $L^2$ under any normalizing scale. Instead, we linearize the functional directly in the target distribution, obtaining an influence-function expansion with a remainder controlled by the transport-map error. The influence function is characterized by a linear elliptic partial differential equation. Under regularity conditions, we use this expansion to prove central limit theorems in low dimensions and establish validity of the empirical bootstrap. We also derive semiparametric efficiency bounds and show that the plug-in estimators attain them under the same conditions.

papers.title: Flavor decomposition of electromagnetic multipole moments in $[q_1q_2][\bar q_3 \bar c]$ tetraquarks: Light-quark analogs of $T_{cs1}(2900)^0$ with $J^P = 1^+$
papers.summary: We present a systematic study of the magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments of compact $[q_1 q_2][\bar q_3 \bar c]$ tetraquark states with quantum numbers $J^P = 1^+$, in the diquark--antidiquark picture and within the light-cone QCD sum rule framework. By performing a flavor decomposition across all admissible $u/d$ configurations, we show that the charm-quark contribution to the electromagnetic moments vanishes algebraically at the operator level -- a structural feature of the specific spin organization adopted here, in which the heavy antiquark resides in a pseudoscalar antidiquark, distinct from the dynamical $1/m_c$ suppression operative in alternative compact constructions and in hadronic molecules. The magnetic moments follow a coherent light-flavor pattern -- positive for $uu$-, negative for $dd$-, and suppressed for mixed-flavor diquarks -- and the quadrupole moments are non-zero throughout, corresponding, in the customary geometrical interpretation, to intrinsically deformed charge distributions. We further identify the dimensionless multipole ratio $\mathcal{D}/μ$ as a structural observable, independent of the normalization of the interpolating current, which probes the relative geometry of the spin-current and charge distributions complementary to the absolute moments. Taken together, the algebraic decoupling of the charm contribution and the operator-level distinction it implies among different singly-heavy tetraquark architectures constitute methodological signatures that discriminate among the corresponding internal organizations and, to the extent that a physical candidate is dominated by one of them, among compact and molecular interpretations.
papers.comment: 12 pages, 5 tables,1 figure. The version is accepted for publication in Physics Letters B

papers.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
papers.summary: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

papers.title: Parameter dependence of the mapping of the mean-field Ising model onto QCD in the first-order phase transition regime
papers.summary: We map the mean-field Ising equation of state onto the QCD phase diagram and investigate how scaling parameters alter the metastable and unstable regions, as well as the symmetrized pressure and density along an isotherm on the QCD $T-μ_B$ phase plane. We find that, for both the conventional mapping scheme and the scheme valid in the small-quark-mass limit, increasing the scaling parameters $w$ and $ρ$ narrows the metastable and unstable regions. In the small-quark-mass-limit scheme, larger $w$ and $ρ$ reduce both the Ising-symmetrized pressure and density. For the conventional scheme, increasing $w$ reduces these quantities, while increasing $ρ$ raises the Ising-symmetrized pressure and has only a small effect on the density.

papers.title: PhonoBridge: Error-Aware Phoneme-Mediated EMG-to-Text Reconstruction
papers.summary: Electromyography (EMG) provides a non-invasive means of decoding silently articulated speech into text, but accurate decoding remains challenging due to limited availability of paired EMG-text data. We introduce PhonoBridge, a two-stage framework comprising a channel-aware EMG-to-phoneme frontend and a large language model (LLM) backend for text reconstruction. The frontend is trained on paired EMG-text data that consists of channel-wise feature extraction, cross-channel fusion, and electrode embeddings. With phonemes as the intermediate representation, we expand the backend's training data by converting LibriSpeech transcripts into phoneme-text pairs without additional EMG recordings. To adapt the LLM to frontend noise, we introduce Error-Profile-Guided Augmentation (EPGA), which perturbs transcript-derived phoneme sequences according to error patterns estimated from frontend predictions, generating additional training pairs for the LLM. On the Open Vocabulary silent-speech dataset, PhonoBridge achieves 24.77% WER, outperforming the previously reported best of 28.27% on the same test split.

papers.title: CAESAR: Mixed Reality Search-and-Rescue Platform for Cognitive Attack Evaluation
papers.summary: Mixed Reality (MR) enables immersive training by tightly coupling virtual content with the physical environment and supporting embodied interaction. In safety-critical collaborative tasks such as search-and-rescue, however, users rely heavily on virtual elements for perception, coordination, and decision-making, making them vulnerable to cognitive attacks that subtly distort visual feedback, virtual content, or system synchronization. While prior MR security research has examined individual attack mechanisms, evaluations are typically conducted in isolated or single-user settings, and there is a lack of standardized collaborative testbeds for systematic adversarial experimentation. In this paper, we develop CAESAR, an end-to-end multi-user MR framework for systematic evaluation of cognitive attacks in collaborative search-and-rescue training. CAESAR features a modular architecture that integrates four classes of cognitive attacks within a synchronized collaborative scenario and incorporates a multimodal data collection pipeline that captures behavioral, performance, and subjective measures under adversarial conditions. We conduct a controlled user study with an in-depth analysis of the latency-based attack, demonstrating measurable effects on task performance and user behavior while characterizing users' subjective experience under adversarial conditions.
papers.comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR) and selected for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG) special issue

papers.title: BARRR: Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression for Multi-View Multi-Cohort Data
papers.summary: Bidimensional data integration across multiple cohorts (i.e., sample groups) and views (i.e., sources or modalities) is crucial in biomedical research to derive holistic insights from heterogeneous datasets. However, most existing integrative methods focus on a single dimension, such as multi-view integration across distinct sources or multi-cohort integration across distinct sample groups. Existing approaches for bidimensional integration are scarce and predominantly unsupervised, overlooking the valuable insights offered by covariates. To address this gap, we introduce the Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression (baRRR) method. Our approach models covariate-related and unrelated effects concurrently, while also decomposing effect levels (global, partially shared, and individual) across both dimensions. Extensive simulations demonstrate the advantages of our method with respect to signal recovery, outcome prediction, and missing data imputation. We apply our approach to data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), using somatic mutations as covariates to inform patterns of variability across different omics platforms and cancer types. These studies highlight its potential as a robust and adaptable tool for integrative analysis in biomedical research.

papers.title: A Radiation-Hardened, Fault-Aware Quantized Neural Network That Self-Heals
papers.summary: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly being deployed into radiation-challenging environments in spacecraft, particle accelerators, and, soon, space-based data centers. Instantiated as a learned orchestration of numbers stored in persistent memory, models are susceptible to continual degradation as high-energy particles corrupt data. At inference time, new data passed through the network fundamentally break the off-line assumptions and guarantees of a static model determined during training. To preserve the quality and efficacy of the models, fault tolerance against bit flips is a clear objective. In this work we developed a runtime method for repairing the quantized weights of neural networks (NNs) after bit flips on commodity, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware, without storing extra replicas. Our work extends the well-established Fault-Aware Training (FAT) paradigm by adding an alignment penalty to concentrate undamaged activations and weights into a low-rank subspace, and we then reconstruct flagged corrupted coordinates from the uncorrupted survivors. We call this method {\it Projection Healing} and apply it to six regression benchmarks on quantized NNs. Holding a FAT checkpoint fixed and toggling only the runtime heal gives a further ${\sim}23\%$ reduction in the native-unit excess integral. Across those datasets the method extends the operational scrub interval by a median of $2.04\times$ at a $+5\%$ RMSE degradation and $1.96\times$ at $+50\%$, compared with $1.62\times$ and $1.07\times$ for classical Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED). This introduces a new path towards designing resilient data-driven models, complementing established hardware redundancy, ECC, and FAT-based techniques.

papers.title: What should AI forget? A design and taxonomy for negative space governance in AI memory
papers.summary: AI memory personalizes assistants, yet users want some disclosed information forgotten. We characterize the negative space of AI memory, where protection should take precedence over potential future personalization benefits. From 179 incidents reported by 146 users, we developed a taxonomy of 15 information categories users want excluded from memory, revealing sensitivity concerns beyond conventional taxonomies. We operationalize this taxonomy in FENCE, a policy-level memory gate that automatically applies user-selected category-based rules to subsequent conversations, preventing information from protected conversations from entering AI memory by default while allowing case-by-case overrides. In a within-subjects study (N=15), participants described FENCE as making memory governance more usable, interpretable, and trustworthy than conventional post-hoc management. Our findings demonstrate how taxonomy-based rules can potentially support user-defined memory boundaries. We call for collective efforts to establish policies governing what AI should not remember, rather than leaving protection to individual retrospective management.

papers.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

papers.title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
papers.summary: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

papers.title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
papers.summary: Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications. Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

papers.title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
papers.summary: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well, with qualifications. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux \emph{increases} the dependence, consistent with conditioning on a collider, since flux is a joint function of concentrations on both sides of the boundary. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field that thick screens the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.

papers.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
papers.summary: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

papers.title: Caterpillar trees are asymmetric, balanced trees are symmetric
papers.summary: Two conjectures of Allman, Long and Rhodes are proven. The ultrametric exchangeable model captures the symmetries in allele distributions of ultrametric mechanistic models of coalescence and substitution in mathematical phylogeny. The dimension of this model with respect to the species tree leaf count is shown to be greatest for caterpillar trees and least for balanced trees.

papers.title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
papers.summary: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

papers.title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
papers.summary: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.
papers.comment: The first three authors contribute equally to this work

papers.title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
papers.summary: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.

papers.title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
papers.summary: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.
papers.comment: 24 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Benchmark and tasks: https://github.com/Protege-AI/ProteinGeoBench

papers.title: What Language Adds, and at What Cost: Four Controlled Probes of Pathology Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Vision--language models (VLMs) promise to make computational pathology queryable and able to draft reports, but how much language adds beyond the vision backbone is unclear, because almost every system is evaluated by its developers on test sets of their own choosing. We grade published evidence by how it was produced and test four claims with controlled probes that reuse released checkpoints and public data, varying one input at a time. Report text adds prognostic signal: adding a frozen embedding of the stage-redacted report to a slide embedding raises the pooled C-index by 0.019 for progression-free interval and by 0.016 for overall survival across 1{,}633 TCGA patients, and restoring the stage statement adds nothing. Prompts add no measurable accuracy at inference: with features and pooling fixed, zero-shot classification is statistically indistinguishable from a supervised linear probe for lung and renal cancer subtyping. Slide-level question answering is barely grounded: SlideChat answers 74.82\% of SlideBench-VQA(TCGA) items correctly with the slide and 74.41\% without it, whereas its language backbone alone reaches 43.52\%. Paraphrasing leaves accuracy unchanged but flips 8--23\% of answers. Self-reported gains from agentic navigation and few-shot language priors cannot yet be attributed to language. Language thus adds real but narrow value, and we propose minimum controls that would expose these failure modes in future evaluations.

papers.title: Bombadil: A Foundation Model for Plant Electrophysiology
papers.summary: Living plants, like animals, use electrical signals to carry information about their physiological state across their body, from roots to branches. These signals can be recorded, as they are in animals, from a pair of differential extracellular electrodes inserted into signal-conducting tissue. While machine-learning models have been trained to predict specific plant stress states from these signals, each of these models has been trained for only a single task and none have been designed to transfer across tasks, species, or environments. These approaches do not allow easy scaling across the wide range of species and environments that are relevant to agriculture, forestry, and horticulture for both commercial and consumer plant care. Here we present Bombadil, a foundation model for plant electrophysiology, pretrained without labels on over 4 million hours of electrical signals recorded from 100 plant species in ten distinct environments, including laboratories, greenhouses, commercial orchards, and natural forests. In this way, Bombadil is able to learn the fundamental features of plant electrical signals across a wide array of species and environments. Then, from those same electrical signals, Bombadil tracks changes in seven physiological indicators of plant stress, even among species and stressors with no labels in training.
